name: Bass Music
about: "Bass music" is the catch-all that British DJs and writers settled on around 2008 for what came after dubstep's first wave: records built on sub-bass and syncopation that no longer fit garage, grime, dubstep or techno. Its centre was London and Bristol, with Hyperdub, Tectonic, Hessle Audio, Night Slugs and Punch Drunk as the labels, and a cousin in the Los Angeles beat scene around Flying Lotus. Tempos wander between 130 and 170, drums are swung or broken, the low end is the lead instrument and the mood is usually damp and nocturnal. Burial's Untrue is the masterpiece; Joy Orbison, James Blake and Jamie xx carried it toward pop; Objekt, Djrum and Overmono keep it mutating.

artists.name: Kode9
artists.why: Hyperdub founder and the scene's theorist

artists.name: Peverelist
artists.why: Punch Drunk and Livity Sound, Bristol's techno bridge

artists.name: Flying Lotus
artists.why: Brainfeeder and the LA beat scene

albums.title: Burial
albums.why: South London rain, pirate radio static and 2-step rhythms gone spectral; the debut that gave post-garage a melancholy it never shook.

albums.title: Memories of the Future
albums.why: Hyperdub's founder and his dread-voiced poet map dubstep as paranoid science fiction; slow, smoky and still unsettling.

albums.title: Untrue
albums.why: Pitched-up vocal ghosts over shuffling drums, grief and the night bus rendered in sound; the record the whole post-dubstep decade answers to.

albums.title: Underwater Dancehall
albums.why: Bristol's Tectonic boss stretches dubstep toward dub and vocals, issued with an instrumental twin; the city's bass lineage restated for the 2000s.

albums.title: Where Were U in '92?
albums.why: A hardcore-rave pastiche so loving and exact it became a rave record in its own right, and the start of the nostalgia strain in bass music.

albums.title: Jarvik Mindstate
albums.why: Punch Drunk's founder folds techno pulse into dubstep swing with rare restraint; the hinge between Bristol's dubstep and its later Livity Sound years.

albums.title: Three EPs
albums.why: The Skull Disco material gathered for Perlon: hand-drum polyrhythms, sub-bass and muttered dread, closer to Berlin than to Croydon.

albums.title: 5: Five Years of Hyperdub
albums.why: A two-disc summary of the label that defined the sound, pairing new cuts from Burial, Kode9 and Zomby with the catalogue's best; the essential primer.

albums.title: Cosmogramma
albums.why: Los Angeles' beat scene reaches for Alice Coltrane and gets there: harp, free-jazz drums and wobbling low end in one dense, generous suite.

albums.title: Crooks & Lovers
albums.why: Field recordings, guitar loops and half-remembered garage rhythms; the record that made 'post-dubstep' sound like a real place rather than a tag.

albums.title: Splazsh
albums.why: Darren Cunningham's smeared, lo-fi house and techno sketches, a bass record only by association but one the scene claimed immediately.

albums.title: James Blake
albums.why: Dubstep's sub-bass and silence rebuilt around a singer-songwriter's voice; a pop breakthrough that still sounds strange.

albums.title: Glass Swords
albums.why: Maximalist Glasgow bass: prog-synth fanfares, trap drums and slap bass piled high, as joyful as the scene ever got.

albums.title: SBTRKT
albums.why: The masked producer's debut turns post-dubstep rhythms into radio-ready songs with Sampha; polished, likeable and a little safe.

albums.title: Hessle Audio: 116 & Rising
albums.why: Ben UFO, Pangaea and Pearson Sound's label at its peak, a compilation that captured the 130 BPM middle ground between dubstep and house.

albums.title: Dedication
albums.why: Short, mournful miniatures made for 4AD after a bereavement; the rave nostalgist at his most restrained and affecting.

albums.title: Classical Curves
albums.why: Night Slugs' manifesto: gleaming, hollowed-out club tracks that borrow from grime, ballroom and corporate muzak; hugely influential on the decade's club minimalism.

albums.title: Luxury Problems
albums.why: Slowed-down techno sunk in tape murk with his former piano teacher's voice floating above; Modern Love's defining record and a widely imitated one.

albums.title: TNGHT
albums.why: Hudson Mohawke and Lunice's five-track EP of brass stabs and trap drums, the moment bass music and rap production collided for good.

albums.title: Cold Mission
albums.why: Grime deconstructed to gunshots, silence and square-wave bass on Keysound; austere and influential on the 'weightless' school that followed.

albums.title: Flatland
albums.why: A debut of sculpted, mechanical precision that moves between techno, electro and bass without belonging to any; a producer's producer's record.

albums.title: In Colour
albums.why: Rave history, steel drums and garage vocals turned into a gentle, nostalgic pop album; the bass underground's biggest crossover of the decade.

albums.title: Portrait with Firewood
albums.why: Felix Manuel's piano, cello and broken drum programming in a continuous emotional arc; bass music treated as composition.

albums.title: still slipping vol. 1
albums.why: A 'mixtape' of family voicemails and warm, unfinished club sketches from the producer of 'Hyph Mngo'; intimate, if slighter than its reputation.

albums.title: Good Lies
albums.why: The Russell brothers' debut album sets pitched vocal hooks over breaks and sub-bass; the 2020s' most convincing bridge between rave and pop.
